blocks.text: Between two men who were conversing immediately beside the door—one, with both hands stretched far out before him, was making the motions of counting out money, the other was looking him keenly in the eyes—a hand reached for K. It was a small, rosy-cheeked boy. “Come, come,” he said. K. allowed himself to be led by him; it turned out that a narrow passage was nevertheless clear through the milling throng, possibly dividing two parties; this was also suggested by the fact that in the front rows to right and left K. saw scarcely a face turned towards him, but only the backs of people who addressed their speeches and gestures solely to members of their own party. Most were dressed in black, in old Sunday coats hanging long and loose about them. Only these clothes puzzled K., otherwise he would have taken the whole thing for a district political meeting.

At the other end of the hall, to which K. was led, a small table stood crosswise on a very low platform, likewise overcrowded, and behind it, near the edge of the platform, sat a small, fat, puffing man, who was just then conversing amid much laughter with someone standing behind him—the latter had rested his elbow on the back of the chair and crossed his legs. At times he flung his arm into the air as though caricaturing someone. The boy who was leading K. had difficulty delivering his message. Twice already he had stood on tiptoe and tried to communicate something, without being noticed by the man above. Only when one of the people up on the platform drew attention to the boy did the man turn towards him and, bending down, listen to his quiet report. Then he took out his watch and glanced quickly at K. “You ought to have appeared 1 hour and 5 minutes ago,” he said. K. wished to reply, but he had no time, for scarcely had the man finished speaking when a general murmuring arose in the right-hand half of the hall. “You ought to have appeared 1 hour and 5 minutes ago,” the man now repeated in a raised voice, and now also glanced quickly down into the hall. At once the murmuring too grew louder and, as the man said no more, subsided only gradually. It was now much quieter in the hall than when K. had entered. Only the people in the gallery did not cease making their remarks. So far as anything could be distinguished up there in the half-light, haze and dust, they seemed more poorly dressed than those below. Some had brought cushions, which they had placed between their heads and the ceiling to keep themselves from being rubbed sore.

K. had resolved to observe more than to speak, and consequently refrained from defending himself against his alleged lateness and merely said: “I may have come late, but now I am here.” Applause followed, again from the right-hand half of the hall. “People easily won over,” thought K., and was disturbed only by the silence in the left-hand half of the hall, which lay immediately behind him and from which only a few isolated handclaps had arisen. He considered what he might say to win them all over at once or, if that should prove impossible, at least to win the others over from time to time as well.

“Yes,” said the man, “but I am no longer obliged to examine you now”—again the murmuring, though this time its meaning was unclear, for the man continued, waving the people to silence—“I shall nevertheless make an exception and do so today. But such lateness must not occur again. And now step forward!” Someone jumped down from the platform, leaving a place free for K., who stepped up into it. He stood pressed close against the table; the throng behind him was so great that he had to resist its pressure if he was not to push the examining magistrate’s table, and perhaps the magistrate himself, off the platform.
